abstract: Bread wheat is an allohexaploid in which the three homoeologous copies of most genes are expressed unequally, and transposable elements (TEs) occupying gene bodies have been proposed as one source of that imbalance. Previous tests of this idea examined a single genotype, so they could not ask whether differences in insertion between cultivars correspond to differences in expression. We sequenced young-leaf transcriptomes of six bread wheat cultivars, quantified them against IWGSC RefSeq v2.1, and combined them with transposable element annotations generated independently for each cultivar's own genome. Between 29.47% and 29.64% of genes carried an element that lay entirely within the gene body, 85% of which were intronic. Across all 12,887 homoeologous groups analyzed, agreement between insertion and expression exceeded a permutation null only modestly. Restricting the test to the 1,692 groups whose insertion pattern differs between cultivars changed the picture: 115 of these showed expression bias tracking the insertion, against 27.3 expected, a 4.21-fold enrichment. The association was markedly asymmetric, reaching 6.83-fold for suppression of the inserted homoeolog but 2.53-fold for dominance, and it was carried by intronic rather than coding-sequence insertions and by six of eleven element superfamilies. The same trend was observed across all six tissues in an independently generated wheat pan-transcriptome, where quantifying the same reads against each cultivar's own genome assembly confirmed the association independently of the reference used. We identified 74 candidate loci at which polymorphic insertions were associated with consistent transcriptional suppression across all six cultivars. These findings reveal polymorphic TE insertions as a source of evolutionary variation in homoeolog expression, linking genome structural diversity to transcriptional diversification in bread wheat.
